prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not give haloperidol or another typical antipsychotic: severe neuroleptic sensitivity [DLB_2017]
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine, oxybutynin): they worsen cognition and hallucinations
required_recommendations: Diagnose probable DLB (McKeith 2017): dementia with functional decline and all four core features (fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder and parkinsonism), with the hallucinations and fluctuations beginning about 16 months and the functional decline about 4 months before the parkinsonism (dementia before parkinsonism: DLB, not PDD); MIBG and PSG are indicative biomarkers [DLB_2017]

Start a cholinesterase inhibitor for cognition and hallucinations: rivastigmine (oral 1.5 mg twice daily, increased at intervals of at least 2 weeks to 3 to 6 mg twice daily, or the 4.6 mg/24 h patch increased to 9.5 mg/24 h after 4 weeks) or donepezil (5 mg daily, 10 mg after 4 weeks), with an ECG and heart rate before starting and at each dose step because of the syncope and midodrine [DLB_2017]

Record the severe haloperidol reaction as a drug alert and explain it, the fluctuations and the hallucinations to the family; if an antipsychotic becomes necessary despite the cholinesterase inhibitor, use low-dose quetiapine or clozapine (with blood count monitoring) [DLB_2017]

Treat the orthostatic hypotension: fluids, salt, slow rising, head-up tilt of the bed and compression garments; continue midodrine with the last dose at least 4 hours before bedtime and check supine blood pressure

Make the bedroom safe for dream enactment (separate beds or padding, sharp objects removed) because he has struck his wife; melatonin can be increased, and is preferred to clonazepam given the cognitive impairment and falls

Full vertical eye movements; the two falls were syncopal on standing, not unprovoked postural falls; normal midbrain on MRI
Orthostatic hypotension is present, but early dementia and hallucinations argue against MSA, and there are no cerebellar signs, stridor or putaminal, pontine or cerebellar peduncle change on MRI

key_clinical_evidence: Dementia with functional decline: his wife now manages his finances and medications and he has stopped driving; MoCA 19/30 and MMSE 23/30 with attention, executive and visuospatial deficits

Four core features: fluctuating cognition and alertness (observed during the exam), recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder by history, and parkinsonism (symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity): probable DLB [DLB_2017]
The cognitive and psychiatric symptoms began about 16 months before the parkinsonism, and RBD a year before them: DLB rather than PDD by the one-year rule

Reduced DaT uptake, low cardiac MIBG uptake and PSG-confirmed REM sleep without atonia are indicative biomarkers; with four core features they add certainty but are not needed

alternatives: Donepezil, with the same bradycardia precautions.
contraindications: Haloperidol and other D2-blocking antipsychotics and antiemetics: a severe reaction to haloperidol 0.5 mg is recorded 3 months ago.
interactions: Rivastigmine is vagotonic: bradycardia and syncope are possible, and midodrine can cause reflex bradycardia; check the ECG and heart rate before starting and at each dose step.
Mirtazapine, like other antidepressants, can induce or aggravate REM sleep without atonia and dream enactment.
general.summary: Cholinesterase inhibitor with midodrine: additive bradycardia; ECG and heart-rate check advised. Recorded haloperidol reaction: avoid D2 blockers.
warnings: Midodrine causes supine hypertension: give the last dose at least 4 hours before bedtime and check supine blood pressure.
Mirtazapine adds sedation to the daytime drowsiness; use the lowest effective dose.
Melatonin: no clinically relevant interaction with rivastigmine.

metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Differentiating dementia with Lewy bodies from Parkinson disease in a patient referred with a PD diagnosis but whose cognitive/psychiatric symptoms preceded motor symptoms
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Referred with a PD label, the patient meets probable DLB on history and examination: the agent must place the cognitive symptoms before the parkinsonism, read the haloperidol reaction as neuroleptic sensitivity and the syncope as orthostatic. metadata.key_teaching_point: When dementia with visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition and RBD begins before or within a year of the parkinsonism, the diagnosis is DLB rather than PD or PDD; reduced DaT uptake does not separate the two

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Kenji Takahashi is a 68-year-old right-handed retired architect who is referred to the neurology movement disorders clinic by his primary care physician for evaluation of 'Parkinson's disease.' His PCP noted bilateral tremor and rigidity at a routine visit 4 months ago and made a provisional diagnosis of PD. His wife, who accompanies him and provides the bulk of the history, paints a more complex picture. Approximately 2 years ago, Mr. Takahashi began experiencing vivid, detailed visual hallucinations. He sees children playing in the living room, a cat sleeping on the bed, and occasionally a woman standing in the corner of the bedroom. Initially he recognized these as unreal and would remark 'there are the children again,' but over the past 6 months he has begun interacting with the hallucinations — reaching out to pet the cat, setting a place at the dinner table for the woman, and becoming distressed when his wife tells him they are not real. Around the same time the hallucinations began, his wife noticed dramatic fluctuations in his cognitive state. Some days he is nearly his normal self — sharp, conversational, able to read the newspaper and discuss current events. Other days, and sometimes even within the same day, he becomes profoundly confused, stares blankly for hours, cannot follow simple instructions, and appears drowsy and disengaged despite adequate sleep. These fluctuations are unpredictable and have no clear trigger. Over the past year his wife has taken over the household finances and his medications because he repeatedly made errors with both, and he stopped driving after getting lost on a familiar route. REM sleep behavior disorder was diagnosed 3 years ago when his wife reported that he was acting out vivid dreams — punching, kicking, and shouting in his sleep. On two occasions he struck his wife during sleep. He was started on melatonin with partial improvement. Motor symptoms are a more recent development. Approximately 8 months ago, his wife noticed that his movements had become slower, his writing smaller, and he was walking with shorter steps. He has bilateral mild rigidity and bradykinesia. Notably, she has NEVER observed a resting tremor — only a mild tremor when he holds his hands out. He has had two falls in the past 6 months with brief loss of consciousness, both while standing from a seated position. These were attributed to 'vasovagal syncope' by his cardiologist after a normal echocardiogram and Holter monitor, but his wife notes the orthostatic hypotension was documented on both occasions. Most concerning to the family was an episode 3 months ago when his PCP prescribed haloperidol 0.5 mg for the hallucinations. Within 48 hours, Mr. Takahashi became severely rigid, nearly unable to move, obtunded, and had to be taken to the emergency department. The haloperidol was discontinued and he recovered over several days, but the family was frightened. His PCP subsequently referred him to neurology. He denies urinary incontinence. His constipation has been present for 4 years.

neurological_exam.additional: Orthostatic vital signs: supine BP 134/78 mmHg, HR 64; standing at 3 minutes BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 70 (systolic fall of 22 mmHg and diastolic fall of 10 mmHg, with a heart-rate rise of 6/min). Patient reports lightheadedness on standing. No inspiratory stridor. Mild myoclonus in both hands observed intermittently. Wife reports she has witnessed 'whole-body jerks' during sleep.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin mildly slow bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements mildly slow and decremented bilaterally, symmetric.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial expression mildly hypomimic bilaterally. Hearing intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly wide-based gait. Slightly shuffling steps with reduced stride length bilaterally. Mildly reduced arm swing bilaterally, symmetric. Tandem gait with 2 missteps in 10 steps. Pull test: mild retropulsion, recovers in 2 steps. No freezing. Turns performed en bloc.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Fluctuating attention during the exam: for the first 10 minutes he is alert, conversational, and engaged, then becomes drowsy, stares blankly for several minutes, and gives slow incoherent responses before spontaneously becoming lucid again. When lucid: oriented to person, place, and situation but misses the exact date by 3 days. MMSE 23/30: lost 2 points on recall (1/3 words, retrieved 1 with category cue), 3 points on serial sevens (3 errors, appeared to lose focus midway), 1 point on orientation (date) and 1 point on the intersecting pentagons (spatial arrangement of the copy lost). MoCA 19/30: visuospatial/executive 2/5 (cube copy failed, clock 2/3 with the numbers clustered on the right half of the face, trail-making 0/1), naming 3/3, attention 4/6 (digit span forward only 4 digits, serial 7s with 3 errors), language 2/3 (phonemic fluency 7 words), abstraction 1/2, delayed recall 2/5 (1 more with category cue), orientation 5/6 (date).
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk throughout. Tone: mild bilateral cogwheel rigidity at wrists, SYMMETRIC — no clear lateralization. Mild bilateral bradykinesia on finger tapping and hand opening-closing, approximately symmetric. NO resting tremor observed during 15-minute observation period. Mild action tremor (postural) in both hands. Strength 5/5 throughout all extremities. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, and patellar bilaterally. Achilles reflexes 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No frontal release signs.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Vibration sense intact at great toes bilaterally. Proprioception intact. No cortical sensory deficits.
